analysis.one_liner: Applies Social Security payroll taxes to all wages, removing the cap for high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a single hearing, vote, or cosponsor: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee in April 2015 and never acted on before the 114th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Social Security is funded by a 6.2% payroll tax on wages, but only up to a cap — $118,500 in 2015. Every dollar above that goes untaxed for Social Security. This bill would remove the cap entirely, so high earners and their employers would pay Social Security tax on all wages, extending the program's solvency without cutting benefits or raising taxes on anyone earning under the cap.
analysis.who_benefits: Social Security beneficiaries, who gain added program solvency without benefit cuts, and the roughly 94% of workers whose wages fall entirely below the cap and would pay no new tax. High earners would pay more, but high earners are a small, concentrated group.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Social Security beneficiaries and workers under the wage cap

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 'contribution and benefit base' — the wage cap (set at $118,500 in 2015) above which wages are exempt from Social Security's 6.2% payroll tax — for both employees and employers [S2] [S3].
Extends the same full-tax treatment to self-employment income, removing the cap there as well [S3].
Applies to wages paid after December 31, 2015, raising revenue that would extend the solvency of the Social Security trust funds, which face projected shortfalls in the 2030s.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and wealthy households, who would pay the 6.2% employee share on all wages above the cap, plus the businesses that employ them, which would pay the matching 6.2% employer share on those wages. Self-employed high earners would pay the full 12.4% on income above the cap.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners above the wage cap

drawbacks.text: High earners would face a substantial tax increase: someone earning $500,000 a year would pay roughly $23,600 more in employee-side Social Security tax, and their employer would pay a matching amount, which could dampen hiring at the top of the pay scale.

Removing the cap entirely breaks the traditional link between what high earners pay in and what they receive from Social Security; critics argue that weakens the program's character as an earned benefit and could invite political attacks on it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — closing most of Social Security's long-term funding gap by taxing top wages — is large and falls entirely on a small, high-income group. The cost is real for high earners and their employers, and the design choice to remove the cap entirely (rather than partially) is aggressive, which likely contributed to the bill drawing no cosponsors. But the core trade-off — program solvency funded by top wages versus a tax increase limited to the top slice of earners — favors the bill for ordinary working people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; it died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Tonko introduced the bill on April 28, 2015 [S1] [S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its two years in Congress [S4].
The committee held no hearing or markup, and the full House never voted on the bill; its only recorded actions are the introduction and the committee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners above the wage cap and the businesses that employ them are better off, since the tax never took effect. So are the members of the Ways and Means Committee, who were spared a vote on taxing top wages.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, who never faced the tax

sides.party_line_note: The bill never drew a vote or a cosponsor from either party, so no partisan breakdown of support exists; the sponsor was a Democrat and the committee that ignored it had a Republican majority in the 114th Congress.

industries.note: Wages above $118,500 would have become subject to the 6.2% Social Security tax for both employee and employer. This concentrated group's gain came from the bill dying.

industries.industry: Large employers of high earners (finance, tech, professional services)
industries.note: Employers would pay the matching 6.2% share on high salaries. Because the bill died, they avoid that cost.
The added payroll tax revenue would have extended the trust funds' solvency, strengthening retirement and disability benefits for ordinary workers. That support never arrived.
